title: Higher-order Parity Constraints for Quantum Approximate Optimization
authors: Anita Weidinger, Glen Bigan Mbeng, Roeland ter Hoeven, Wolfgang Lechner
abstract: The Parity Architecture was originally introduced in the context of quantum optimization algorithms to overcome hardware connectivity constraints. Here, we show that its benefits extend beyond this role by identifying specific parity transformations that enhance the success probability of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for optimization problems defined on hardware-native and sparse graphs. Numerical simulations suggest that this enhancement originates from the higher-order operators introduced by the Parity representation, which accelerate the propagation of correlations across the physical device. We investigate this mechanism for the Signed Max-Cut problem on 3-regular graph instances and demonstrate its practical relevance on IBM Heron quantum processors. QAOA parameters are first classically optimized on small training instances containing up to 14 vertices and subsequently transferred to larger instances executed on quantum hardware. We consider Signed Max-Cut instances of up to 40 vertices and find that, together with an error mitigation technique, the parity-based QAOA identifies the optimal solutions for all the considered 40-vertex instances, whereas the conventional QAOA fails under the same conditions.
summary: This paper proposes using a Parity Architecture to enhance the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for solving optimization problems like Signed Max-Cut. By identifying specific parity transformations, the authors show that the resulting algorithm can effectively propagate correlations across sparse graphs, achieving optimal solutions where standard QAOA fails on larger instances. This work advances the practical application of quantum algorithms by addressing underlying physical constraints.
main_problem: The paper aims to enhance the success probability of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for solving optimization problems on hardware-native and sparse graphs.
main_result: The parity-based QAOA successfully identifies optimal solutions for 40-vertex Signed Max-Cut instances, whereas the conventional QAOA fails under the same conditions when error mitigation is applied.
method: The authors employ a parity transformation to map the problem Hamiltonian into a form solvable by QAOA, utilizing higher-order parity constraints to accelerate correlation propagation.
model_or_system: The work focuses on the Signed Max-Cut problem, modeled by a problem Hamiltonian $H_P$, and implemented on quantum hardware, specifically tested on IBM Heron processors.
key_observables: Success Probability (PGS), circuit depth, and covering depth ($c_p$).
important_parameters: The number of vertices (up to 40), the QAOA parameters $( eta, \gamma)$, and the graph structure (e.g., 3-regular graphs).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the applicability of parity constraints to extend QAOA benefits beyond mere hardware connectivity, and relies on classical optimization of QAOA parameters.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mapping of graphs (like the heavy-hex graph) into logical and parity representations, and plot the PGS versus two-qubit gate depth comparing the two QAOA variants.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the parity transformation and the resulting Hamiltonian structure, compares the performance metrics (like covering depth) against conventional QAOA, and concludes with numerical results on large instances.
why_interesting: The explicit comparison of algorithmic depth metrics (covering depth vs. gate depth) and the demonstration of superior performance on hard instances makes this highly relevant for quantum algorithm design.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Heavy-hex graph with N = 21 nodes in its logical (a) and Parity (b) representation. Interactions in the logical graph can be implemented via Rzz gates and constraints in the Parity graph with CNOT and Rzz gates, shown next to the graphs in (c). Panel (d) shows the best found parameters for p ∈{1, 2, 3} during optimization. Parameters at p = 1 are denoted by a single marker, while parameters at p = 2 and p = 3 with two or three markers that are connected via a dashed and solid line, respectively.

FIG. 2. Ground state probability PGS of noiseless simulations (grey) and hardware experiments on ibm torino (colored) as a function of the two-qubit gate depth for a heavy-hex graph of N = 21 nodes. The first marker correspond to p = 1, the second marker to p = 2 and so on. Best parameters obtained from the classical simulations were used for a single job with 4096 measurements. For Parity QAOA one spanning tree M = 1 is used for decoding. For the green line Parity’ the first constraint unitary is applied despite Ω1 = 0, showing the impact of noise from the additional constraint layer.

FIG. 3. Two-qubit gate depth and two-qubit gate count (with Rzz gates) for the first entangling layer of random 3-regular graphs on a square grid (a) and on a heavy-hex topology (b). The top panel in (c) shows the covering depth cp and the bottom panel shows the number of qubits in the entangling gates (constraints, interactions). Panel (d) shows the total two-qubit gate depth (two-qubit gate depth multiplied by cp) and total two-qubit gate count needed to cover the whole graph on a square grid layout.

FIG. 4. 3-regular graph with N = 14 nodes in its (a) logical and (b) Parity representation. Panel (c) shows the average of the best found parameters for both QAOA variants. Parameters for p = 1 are presented with a single marker and for p = 2 and p = 3 the markers are connect by a dashed and solid, respectively. Error bars denote the standard deviation.

FIG. 5. Ground state probability PGS obtained from experiments on the ibm fez machine for 3-regular graphs of size (a) N = 14 , (b) N = 30 and (c) N = 40. The solid lines denote the average over 12 random instances for (a) and 20 random instances for (b) and (c), error bars denote the standard deviation. The first marker correspond to p = 1, the second marker to p = 2 and so on. Results from noiseless simulations for N = 14 are represented by gray lines in (a), square markers for parity and dots for the direct implementation.
